ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Four participants voluntarily withdrew from the study due to personal reasons unrelated to the study procedures.

> Recruited participants were healthy individuals aged above 18 years.

> All participants provided written informed consent and completed PAR-Q before participation.

> Before each visit, participants completed a 24-hour food log and refrained from vigorous exercise, caffeine and alcohol for 24 hours.

> Participants were instructed to pinch their noses during consumption to minimise olfactory cues.

> Participants were told to maintain their habitual diet, avoid consumption of other supplements throughout the study, and abstain from caffeine consumption 24 hours before testing sessions.

> Three of the twenty participants were regular caffeine consumers at 100-300 mg⋅day⁻¹.

> Participants were instructed to press the spacebar as quickly as possible when a smiley or winky face appeared on the screen (Figure 2).

> Participants were required to respond to a smiley face (Go trial) by pressing the The number of trials using Smiley and Winkey faces, and the number of specific inter-trial intervals were shown.

> The absence of pharmacokinetic data from the guarana doses and caffeine in our participants prevents confirmation of temporal effects of interventions on central activation, which is crucial for interpreting psychostimulant studies (62).

> Additionally, our participant cohort were primarily young healthy adults which limits the generalisability of the findings as the cognitive benefits of guarana's constituents have been observed in ageing and clinical populations, including individuals with cognitive diseases such as Alzheimer's (63,64), highlighting the need for further research to assess guarana's effects within these groups.

> Although many participants were tested at consistent times, several completed assessments at varying time points, introducing potential time-of-day effects.

> Participants were instructed to press the spacebar in response to a winky face (Go trial) and 156 to withhold response to a smiley face (Stay trial).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.
